warmup.q: merchants.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { m -> val fee = feeService.lookup(m); flowOf(fee) } runs over 10 merchants. Each lookup suspends for 100 ms. How long does it take?
options: 1,000 ms: one lookup at a time
It doesn't compile: the lambda must not suspend
warmup.why: flatMapMerge calls the lambda sequentially, in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, before it takes a lane. A lookup inside the lambda therefore runs one merchant at a time. Only the returned flows run concurrently, so flow { emit(feeService.lookup(m)) } would give the 300 ms you expected.

sections.h: Your flatMapMerge lambda runs one value at a time
sections.html:
Ten merchants are waiting for their fees. The fee service allows 4 concurrent calls, and a lookup takes 100 ms. This code is supposed to fan out 4 at a time. The trace shows one call at a time, 1,000 ms in all:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's flatMap with a blocking call in the mapper
merchants.flatMap(merchant -> {
    Fee fee = feeService.lookupBlocking(merchant);   // 100 ms on the calling thread
    return Mono.just(fee);
}, 4);
Kotlin
merchants.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { merchant ->
    val fee = feeService.lookup(merchant)        // a suspend call, 100 ms
    flowOf(fee)
}

To see why, build the operator yourself. It takes three parts: a coroutine that reads the outer flow, a semaphore with one permit per lane, and one coroutine per inner flow, all sending into one channel:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: one loop builds each task, a semaphore caps the lanes, one virtual thread per lane
static void mergeLanes(List<String> merchants, int lanes, BlockingQueue<Fee> out) throws InterruptedException {
    Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(lanes);
    for (String m : merchants) {
        Callable<Fee> inner = () -> feeService.lookupBlocking(m);   // built here, one merchant at a time
        permits.acquire();                                         // wait for a free lane
        Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
            try { out.put(inner.call()); } catch (Exception e) { /* omitted */ } finally { permits.release(); }
        });
    }
}
Kotlin
fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mergeLanes(lanes: Int, transform: suspend (T) -> Flow<R>): Flow<R> = channelFlow {
    val permits = Semaphore(lanes)
    collect { value ->
        val inner = transform(value)          // runs here, one value at a time
        permits.acquire()                     // wait for a free lane
        launch { try { inner.collect { send(it) } } finally { permits.release() } }
    }
}

Now read the bug again. transform runs inside the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, before it even asks for a permit. Whatever you do in the lambda happens one merchant at a time. Only the flow it returns gets a lane of its own. So the slow call has to live inside that flow: flatMapMerge(4) { m -> flow { emit(feeService.lookup(m)) } }. With five merchants of 300, 100, 200, 50 and 150 ms and two lanes, that version finishes at 450 ms with 2 in flight. The lambda version takes 800 ms, the same as a plain map { lookup(it) }.

The library's flatMapMerge is map(transform).flattenMerge(concurrency), and flattenMerge is the same shape as mergeLanes: a producer coroutine, a Semaphore(concurrency), a launch per inner flow, and one output channel of 64 slots. Its KDoc says it "calls transform sequentially". Results come out in completion order: m2, m1, m3, m4, m5. Picture a toll plaza with N booths feeding one merge lane. One dispatcher at the entrance waves cars in, one at a time. If he inspects every car himself, the booths sit empty.

Without a concurrency argument you get DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY, which is 16, read once from the property kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency. Reactor's flatMap defaults to 256. In 1.11.0 flatMapMerge is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi and DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY is @FlowPreview. Without an opt-in you get a compiler warning, not an error. Set the cap from the provider's contract, never from the default.

Check yourself: in the fixed version with two lanes, at what time does the lambda run for m3?

static { LATENCY.put("m1", 300L); LATENCY.put("m2", 100L); LATENCY.put("m3", 200L); LATENCY.put("m4", 50L); LATENCY.put("m5", 150L); } static final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(); static final AtomicInteger maxInFlight = new AtomicInteger(); } // a blocking lookup, called in the mapper: the wait happens before flatMap gets a publisher static String lookupNow(String m) { started(m); try { Thread.sleep(LATENCY.get(m)); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } inFlight.decrementAndGet(); return m + ":fee"; } static void scenario(String title, Flux<String> fees) { if (!quiet) System.out.println("== " + title); maxInFlight.set(0); t0 = System.nanoTime(); fees.doOnNext(f -> log("subscriber got " + f)).blockLast(); } }

Results arrive m2, m1, m3, m4, m5 and the run ends at 450 ms with 2 in flight. The lambda version ends at 800 ms with 1 in flight. mergeLanes matches the first scenario exactly. Reactor gives about 450 ms with Mono.delay inside the returned Mono, and about 800 ms when the mapper blocks before returning Mono.just.

sections.h: The outer flow waits in flatMapConcat, and flatMapLatest drops the old lane
sections.html:
A merchant search box gets three picks, 100 ms apart. For each pick, a details flow sends part a after 50 ms and part b 150 ms later. With flatMapConcat, at what time does the outer flow emit pick 2?

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: concatMap (and flatMap, switchMap) on the same Flux timeline
picks().concatMap(n -> details(n));
Kotlin
picks().flatMapConcat { n -> details(n) }     // also try flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest

Most people say 100. It is 300, and the whole run takes 800 ms. flatMapConcat is map(transform).flattenConcat(), and flattenConcat is one line: collect { value -> emitAll(value) }. No coroutine, no channel. The inner flow runs inside the outer's emit, so the outer's code is paused until the inner has finished, and its delay(100) only starts after that. Picture a single-lane bridge where the depot worker drives each truck across himself. No new truck gets loaded while one is on the bridge. Put buffer() in front, and the outer runs in its own coroutine and loads trucks into a parking lot. The run drops to 600 ms.

Reactor's concatMap on the same timeline also finishes at 600 ms. It asks for one item at a time too, but the timers in its source kept running while no request was outstanding. A flow { } body can't do that: it is suspended in emit. If you want Reactor's timeline in Flow, add the buffer().

flatMapMerge gives each pick its own lane. The outer emits at 0, 100 and 200, the inner values interleave by completion time (1-b at 200 comes after 2-a at 150), and the run ends at 400.

flatMapLatest is a railway switch that drops the old lane. It is transformLatest { emitAll(transform(it)) }, the operator from lesson 4 of this track. Each new pick cancels the inner in flight with ChildCancelledException ("Child of the scoped flow was cancelled"), joins it, and starts the next. So 1-b and 2-b never arrive, and the run ends at 400. Reactor's switchMap gives the identical timeline. This is the shape for search-as-you-type: a new keystroke makes the old search worthless. Keep the cancelled inner's cleanup short, because the next one waits for it.

The figure shows all three, drawn from the virtual-time output of the Try it.

Check yourself: the outer is for (n in 1..3) { emit(n); delay(100) } and each inner is one value after 200 ms. How long does flatMapConcat take?

sections.h: A zipper for zip, a board of latest values for combine
sections.html:
Checkout prices arrive in USD every 100 ms, starting at 100 ms. The USD to EUR rate arrives at 250 ms (0.92) and at 550 ms (0.95). You want each price in EUR. A teammate writes prices.zip(rates):

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the same three Reactor operators
Flux.zip(prices, rates, EurPrice::new);
Flux.combineLatest(prices, rates, EurPrice::new);
Flux.merge(cardEvents, bankEvents);
Kotlin
prices.zip(rates) { cents, rate -> EurPrice(cents, rate) }       // a zipper
combine(prices, rates) { cents, rate -> EurPrice(cents, rate) }  // a board of latest values
merge(cardEvents, bankEvents)                                     // on-ramps onto one road

zip gives two results: 1000 at 0.92 at 250 ms, and 1010 at 0.95 at 550 ms. Then it ends. It is a zipper: each price tooth must meet a rate tooth, by index, and it stops at the end of the shorter side. The price flow's onCompletion reports AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed. Something else happened too: the second price was emitted at 350 ms, not 200. zip collects the receiver (prices) in the caller's coroutine with no buffer at all, and only the other flow gets a producer coroutine with a rendezvous channel. So each price emit waits until a rate is there to pair with. The slower side sets the pace. Reactor's zip produced the same two pairs, but its price feed kept ticking every 100 ms, because Reactor prefetches. Flow has only the two-flow zip.

Pairing the n-th price with the n-th rate is the wrong question for money. You want the latest rate. That is combine, which keeps a board with one slot per flow. It starts one coroutine per source. Nothing comes out until every slot has a value, and after that every update produces one output. The first result is 1010 at 0.92, at 250 ms: price 1000 was overwritten on the board before any rate existed. Then 1020, 1030 and 1040 at 0.92, then 1040 at 0.95 the moment the new rate lands at 550, then 1050 at 0.95. A source that never emits means no output at all, and combine completes when the other sources complete.

merge is on-ramps joining one road. Card events every 100 ms and bank events every 70 ms come out in arrival order: bank-0 at 70, card-0 at 100, bank-1 at 140, and so on. The merged flow ends when the last source ends, and one source that fails cancels the others.

Check yourself: what does combine emit if the rate flow sends 0.92 at 0 ms, before the first price?

try.expect: zip: 1000@0.92 at 250 and 1010@0.95 at 550, with the second price emitted at 350, and the price flow ending with AbortFlowException. combine: 1010@0.92 at 250 first, then one line per update, ending with 1050@0.95 at 600. With an empty rate feed, combine prints nothing and completes at 600. Reactor's zip gives the same two pairs, but its prices keep coming every 100 ms; its combineLatest matches Flow's combine.

sections.h: A slow collector makes combine skip values and slow its sources
sections.html:
Put a slow collector behind combine. A price feed ticks every 10 ms, ten times, and is combined with one merchant config value. The dashboard that collects the result needs 100 ms per update. What does it see?

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: combineLatest in front of a subscriber that takes one at a time
Flux.combineLatest(ticks, Flux.just("cfg"), (i, cfg) -> i + "/" + cfg)
    .concatMap(v -> render(v).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), 1);
Kotlin
combine(ticks, flowOf("cfg")) { i, cfg -> "$i/$cfg" }
    .collect { render(it); delay(100) }        // the dashboard is slow

Flow delivers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10, at 10, 110, 210, 310, 410 and 510 ms. Reactor's combineLatest delivers all ten, at about 110, 210 and so on up to 1,010 ms. And there is a second effect in Flow: the feed itself slowed down. It needed about 330 ms to emit its ten values, not 100.

The mechanism is the board's mailbox. Each source coroutine sends an update into a channel whose capacity equals the number of flows, here 2, and then calls yield(). The collecting loop takes updates in batches: it reads until it sees a second update from a source it already updated in this batch, overwriting that source's slot each time, and then calls your transform once for the batch. While the dashboard is busy, updates pile up. 2 is overwritten by 3 before anyone takes a photo of the board. Once the mailbox is full, the feed's next send suspends: value 4 waits in send from 40 ms. So combine backpressures its sources and skips values, both at once. Picture a scoreboard and a slow photographer. Updates that land between two photos blur into the last one, and the mailbox in front of the board holds only as many notes as there are slots, so fast sources queue at the mailbox. Reactor's photographer keeps every board state in a queue and develops them all.

It is not plain conflation either. Pure latest-only would give 1 and then 10. If you care, say which one you want:

After combine(...) The dashboard sees
nothing 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10 and the feed slows
.conflate() 1 at 10 ms, then 10 at 110 ms
.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED) all ten, the last at 1,010 ms

For FX on a dashboard, skipping is fine. For anything you must audit, every combination counts, and an unbounded buffer is a memory bill you must size yourself.

One more thing not to rely on. Two flows with no delays, combine(flowOf("a0", "a1", "a2"), flowOf("b0", "b1", "b2")), give a0b0, a1b1, a2b2 in Flow and a2b0, a2b1, a2b2 in Reactor. With synchronous sources, the combinations you get depend on scheduling.

Check yourself: with the dashboard at 100 ms per update, would buffer(10) instead of UNLIMITED keep all ten?

code.title: SlowBoard.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.currentCoroutineContext import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.combine import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.conflate import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onEach import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestCoroutineScheduler import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest @OptIn(kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private suspend fun now() = currentCoroutineContext()[TestCoroutineScheduler]!!.currentTime private suspend fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format(now(), msg)) // A price feed ticks every 10 ms (10 ticks); the merchant config is one value. // The dashboard that collects the board needs 100 ms per update. private fun ticks(verbose: Boolean) = flow { for (i in 1..10) { delay(10); if (verbose) log(" feed emits $i"); emit(i) } } fun main() { runTest { println("== combine, slow collector") combine(ticks(verbose = true), flowOf("cfg")) { i, c -> "$i/$c" } .collect { log("-> $it (dashboard busy 100 ms)"); delay(100) } log("done") } runTest { println("== combine(...).conflate(), slow collector") combine(ticks(verbose = false), flowOf("cfg")) { i, c -> "$i/$c" }.conflate() .collect { log("-> $it"); delay(100) } } runTest { println("== combine(...).buffer(UNLIMITED), slow collector") val got = combine(ticks(verbose = false), flowOf("cfg")) { i, c -> "$i/$c" } .buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED).onEach { delay(100) }.toList() log("got ${got.size}: $got") } }

alt.html: package workbench.flows.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's combineLatest in front of a dashboard that needs 100 ms // per update and asks for one at a time. Real time; the rounded column is the model. public class SlowBoardJava { static long t0; static void log(String msg) { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%5d ms (about %4d) %s%n", ms, Math.round(ms / 10.0) * 10, msg); } static Flux<String> board() { Flux<Long> ticks = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(10)).map(i -> i + 1).take(10); return Flux.combineLatest(ticks, Flux.just("cfg"), (i, c) -> i + "/" + c); } public static void main(String[] args) { board().then().block(); // warm up, output ignored System.out.println("== Flux.combineLatest, slow subscriber"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); board().concatMap(v -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(100)).thenReturn(v), 1) .doOnNext(v -> log("-> " + v)) .blockLast(); log("done"); } }

try.expect: Flow's dashboard sees 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10, at 10, 110, 210, 310, 410 and 510 ms. The feed emits 4 at 40 ms and then waits: 5 comes at 120 and 10 at 330. With conflate() it sees 1 at 10 and 10 at 110. With buffer(UNLIMITED) it gets all ten, done at 1,010 ms. buffer(10) also keeps all ten, since ten values fit in 10 slots plus one in hand, while buffer(3) delivers eight (1 to 5, 7, 9, 10): once its slots are full, combine has a slow collector again. Reactor's combineLatest delivers all ten, about 100 ms apart, the last at about 1,050 ms.

refs.title: internal/Combine.kt at tag 1.11.0 (how combine and zip are built)

analogy: Think of road traffic. flatMapConcat is a single-lane bridge where the depot worker drives every truck across himself, so the depot stops loading while a truck is on the bridge. flatMapMerge is a toll plaza: one dispatcher waves cars in one at a time, N booths work in parallel, and cars leave in the order they finish. flatMapLatest is a railway switch that sends the old train to a siding the moment a new one comes, and waits for the old one to stop. zip is a zipper, tooth for tooth. combine is a scoreboard with one slot per source. merge is on-ramps joining a highway. The picture breaks at speed: real traffic has no backpressure. On a Flow road, a slow collector at the end makes the cars upstream stop, and for combine it also blurs some cars into one.
world: Your payment service enriches each authorization with the merchant's fee schedule from a pricing service that allows 4 concurrent calls per client. flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { m -> flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) }.catch { emit(defaultFee(m)) } } respects that contract and keeps one 503 from cancelling the other lookups. The checkout page converts the basket into the customer's currency with combine(basketTotals, fxRates), never zip, because the latest rate is what you quote. The merchant search box uses flatMapLatest so a stale query can't overwrite a fresh one. And the reconciliation job that merges card-network and bank events uses merge, knowing that one feed failing stops both.
mistake: Putting the slow suspend call in the flatMapMerge lambda and returning flowOf(result). It looks concurrent and it compiles without a warning, but the lambda runs in the single coroutine that reads the outer flow, before a lane is taken, so the calls happen one at a time. People make the mistake because Reactor's flatMap reads the same way and the code looks like a map with a cap. In both libraries the fix is the same: the slow work goes inside the returned flow or publisher, flow { emit(lookup(m)) } in Kotlin, Mono.fromCallable or a non-blocking client call in Reactor. If you need one result per item and no concurrency, plain map { lookup(it) } is simpler, and the flatMapMerge KDoc itself recommends it.

compare.title: Flattening and combining in Kotlin Flow and in Reactor

java.title: Reactor
java.html: Flux<Fee> fees = merchants.flatMap(m -> pricing.lookup(m), 4); // default concurrency 256 Flux<Fee> inOrder = merchants.concatMap(m -> pricing.lookup(m)); // source keeps its own timers Flux<Fee> ordered = merchants.flatMapSequential(m -> pricing.lookup(m), 4); Flux<Hit> hits = queries.switchMap(q -> search.find(q)); Flux<Eur> byIndex = Flux.zip(prices, rates, Eur::of); // prefetches both sides Flux<Eur> latest = Flux.combineLatest(prices, rates, Eur::of); // keeps every combination Flux<Evt> events = Flux.merge(cardEvents, bankEvents);

kotlin.title: Kotlin Flow
kotlin.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun pipelines() { val fees = merchants.flatMapMerge(4) { m -> flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) } } // default 16 val inOrder = merchants.flatMapConcat { m -> flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) } } // outer paused in emit // no flatMapSequential: see the worked example val hits = queries.flatMapLatest { q -> search.find(q) } // joins the old inner val byIndex = prices.zip(rates) { p, r -> Eur.of(p, r) } // receiver unbuffered val latest = combine(prices, rates) { p, r -> Eur.of(p, r) } // may skip when slow val events = merge(cardEvents, bankEvents) }

compare.note: The operators line up one for one, and the virtual-time demos give the same timelines for flatMap/flatMapMerge and switchMap/flatMapLatest. The differences come from how each library moves values. In Flow, a value moves by a suspend call, so whatever is upstream of an emit waits for it: flatMapConcat pauses the outer's code (800 ms against Reactor's 600 on the same timeline), and zip slows its receiver to the other side's pace. Reactor moves values on demand and prefetches, so its sources keep their own timers. The defaults differ too: 16 lanes against 256. And with a slow subscriber, combineLatest queues every board state while combine skips some and makes its sources wait. Flow has no built-in flatMapSequential.

worked.title: Fan out fee lookups under a provider contract

steps.say: The pricing service allows 4 concurrent calls. Put the call inside the returned flow, so each merchant gets a lane, and set the cap from the contract. 10 lookups of 100 ms finish at 300 ms.
steps.code: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun fees(merchants: Flow<String>): Flow<Fee> = merchants.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { m -> // 1. the lambda only builds the inner flow flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) } // 2. the slow call runs in the lane }

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: flatMap with a cap, the call inside the returned Mono Flux<Fee> fees(Flux<String> merchants) { return merchants.flatMap(m -> pricing.lookup(m), 4); // lookup returns a lazy Mono }

steps.say: One merchant's lookup fails with a 503. Catch it inside that merchant's inner flow, so only that lane ends with a default. With m1 = 300, m2 = 100 (fails) and m3 = 200 ms, the output is m2's default at 100, m3 at 200 and m1 at 300.
steps.code: merchants.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { m -> flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) } .catch { e -> if (e is IOException) emit(defaultFee(m)) else throw e } // 3. per lane }

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: handle the error inside each inner Mono merchants.flatMap(m -> pricing.lookup(m) .onErrorResume(IOException.class, e -> Mono.just(defaultFee(m))), 4);

steps.say: Compare a catch placed after flatMapMerge. The failing lane cancels its siblings first: m1 and m3 end with JobCancellationException and the caller sees IOException: fee service 503 for m2 at 100 ms. A caught error still ends the upstream, so the catch can only add a fallback after everything else was lost.
steps.code: merchants.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { m -> flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) } } .catch { e -> emit(defaultFee("all")) } // too late: the other lanes are already cancelled

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: onErrorResume after flatMap ends the whole stream merchants.flatMap(m -> pricing.lookup(m), 4) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(defaultFee("all")));

steps.say: The ledger wants the fees back in input order. Flow has no flatMapSequential. Start each call with async, keep up to n of them in flight with a buffer, and await them in order. The buffer(n - 2) counts the buffer's slots plus one Deferred being awaited and one being created, so n must be at least 2. 20 calls of 100 ms take 1,000 / 700 / 500 / 300 ms for n = 2 / 3 / 4 / 8, all in order.
steps.code: fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mapConcurrentOrdered(n: Int, f: suspend (T) -> R): Flow<R> = flow { coroutineScope { this@mapConcurrentOrdered .map { value -> async { f(value) } } // 4. start the call .buffer(n - 2) // 5. at most n started and not yet emitted .collect { emit(it.await()) } // 6. emit in input order } }

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor has it built in Flux<Fee> ordered = merchants.flatMapSequential(m -> pricing.lookup(m), 4);

lab.title: Fan out fee lookups and convert prices at the latest rate
steps: Run the tests once. All 7 fail. The fees tests print the evidence: 1,000 ms instead of 300, and 1 lookup in flight instead of 4.
Fix fees in FanOut.kt without changing the cap. Ask yourself which coroutine runs the lambda.

In feesOrDefault, a catch after flatMapMerge is too late: by then the failing lane has cancelled the other lanes. Put it on the inner flow.

flatMapMerge needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) in 1.11.0. Without it you only get a warning.

drill.title: Write a capped fan-out from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mergeLanes(lanes: Int, transform: suspend (T) -> Flow<R>): Flow<R> with channelFlow, a Semaphore and launch. Then answer: in your version, which line runs one value at a time, and why must the slow call not be in transform?

answer.html: fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mergeLanes(lanes: Int, transform: suspend (T) -> Flow<R>): Flow<R> = channelFlow { val permits = Semaphore(lanes) collect { value -> // 1. one coroutine reads the outer flow val inner = transform(value) // 2. ONE VALUE AT A TIME, before a permit permits.acquire() // 3. wait for a free lane launch { // 4. one coroutine per lane try { inner.collect { send(it) } } // results go into one shared channel finally { permits.release() } } } } // transform runs in the reading coroutine, so a slow call there blocks the next value from // being read at all. Only the flow it returns is collected inside a lane.

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a reading loop, a Semaphore, and a virtual thread per lane static <T, R> void mergeLanes(Iterable<T> outer, int lanes, Function<T, Callable<R>> transform, BlockingQueue<R> out) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(lanes); for (T value : outer) { // 1. one thread reads the outer source Callable<R> inner = transform.apply(value); // 2. one value at a time, before a permit permits.acquire(); // 3. wait for a free lane Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { // 4. one thread per lane try { out.put(inner.call()); } catch (Exception e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { permits.release(); } }); } }

recap: flatMapMerge calls your lambda sequentially, in one producer coroutine, before it takes a lane. Only the returned flows run concurrently, so the slow call belongs inside them.
The cap defaults to 16 (DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY), against Reactor's 256. Set it from the provider's contract. Results come out in completion order.
flatMapConcat runs each inner inside the outer's emit, so the outer's own code pauses. buffer() in front lets it run ahead, which is Reactor's concatMap timeline.
flatMapLatest cancels the old inner, joins it and starts the new one. Use it for search-as-you-type, where stale results are worthless.
zip pairs by index, slows the receiver to the other side's pace and ends with the shorter flow. combine keeps the latest of each and emits once every source has a value. FX conversion is combine.
With a slow collector, combine skips intermediate values and suspends its sources. Add conflate() or buffer() to choose; Reactor's combineLatest keeps them all.

explain.prompt: A teammate's fee fan-out uses flatMapMerge(concurrency = 8), yet the trace shows one pricing call at a time. Explain why, how you'd fix it, and how you'd keep one failing merchant from cancelling the rest. Use the toll plaza picture.
explain.answer: flatMapMerge has one dispatcher at the entrance: a single coroutine reads the merchants and calls the lambda for each, one at a time, before it waves the result into a booth. The booths are the 8 lanes, and only the flow the lambda returns is collected in a booth. The teammate does the pricing call in the lambda itself and returns flowOf(fee), so the dispatcher inspects every car himself and the booths stay empty: one call at a time. The fix is to return flow { emit(pricing.lookup(m)) }, so the call runs inside the lane. To keep a 503 for one merchant from taking the others down, put catch on that inner flow and emit a default fee there. A catch after flatMapMerge comes too late, because the failing lane has already cancelled all the other lanes.

deeper.html:
How far does flatMapMerge run ahead of a slow collector? With 500 one-value inners and a collector stuck on its first value, 82 outer values had been pulled. A plausible split (my inference, not measured) is 64 results in the output channel, about 16 inners suspended on a full channel, and a couple in hand. With .buffer(0) after it the count was 18, and with flatMapConcat it was 1. So budget memory for up to 64 finished results plus concurrency inners. A buffer or flowOn after flatMapMerge fuses into the same channel: flatMapMerge(4) { }.buffer(0) prints as ChannelFlowMerge[concurrency=4, capacity=0].

Edge cases: flatMapMerge(1) returns plain flattenConcat(). flatMapMerge(0) throws IllegalArgumentException: Expected positive concurrency level, but had 0 when you build the flow. Setting -Dkotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency=0 makes the first read of DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY throw ExceptionInInitializerError, caused by IllegalStateException: System property 'kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency' should be in range 1..2147483647, but is '0'. With =4, 40 lookups of 100 ms took 1,000 ms instead of 300.

flattenConcat() and flattenMerge() are the same operators for a Flow<Flow<T>> you already have; flatMapX(f) is literally map(f).flattenX().

The flatMapMerge and flatMapConcat KDoc both say they are discouraged in regular application flows, because "suspending operation in map operator will be sufficient and linear transformations are much easier to reason about". Take that at face value: reach for flatMapMerge when you need bounded concurrency, and for map { suspendCall(it) } when you don't.

combineTransform is combine with a FlowCollector receiver, so the transform can emit zero or several values per board update. Failure works the same way in combine and merge: one source that throws cancels the others (they end with JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling) and the caller gets the original exception.
